ch09.note: Gongsun Daniang (公孙大娘) was the most celebrated sword-dancer of the Tang dynasty; the poet Du Fu (712–770), who as a boy had seen her perform, wrote a famous poem recalling how her sword-dance (‘sword-form’, 剑器, jianqi) held a whole crowd spellbound, the sky and earth themselves seeming to sway with the fall and rise of it. To trace the Emei short-sword form to her lends it a classical, dancer’s grace.

The bagua (八卦), the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes — figures of three broken and unbroken lines standing for the forces of the cosmos — are a common Taoist emblem. Their presence on the scabbard, and the title ‘Reverend’ (道长) by which Huo Tianqing addresses him, mark Dugu Yihe as a Taoist priest: the Emei sword-school of this novel is a Taoist order, seated at the Xuanzhen (‘Dark Truth’) Temple.

The dantian (丹田), the ‘cinnabar field’ a few inches below the navel, is in Chinese medicine and internal alchemy the body’s reservoir of vital breath. To draw on and expel breath from the dantian is the ground of the ‘inner force’ these masters pit against one another; the rare art of doing so while still speaking is what lets the Old Man of Heaven’s Birds talk on through a locked contest of strength.

Chinese mourning was worn in undyed, coarse cloth, hemp or sackcloth, the roughness of the weave graded to the closeness of the tie to the dead. That Huo Tianqing, no kinsman, should put on heavy hempen mourning for Yan Tieshan signals a bond he holds as deep as blood: the debt of a ‘knight of the realm’ to the lord who once honoured him.

ch10.note: The teasing turns on a pun English cannot keep. Hua Manlou’s surname 花 (hua) is the ordinary word for ‘flower’; so when Shi Xiuxue’s every other word is ‘flower,’ her sisters hear her naming him. Sun Xiuqing’s jibe that the girl once swore no flower was half so good to look at as a green vegetable sharpens the joke.

ch10.anchor: much of a kind with vinegar
ch10.note: To ‘eat vinegar’ (吃醋, chi cu) is the set Chinese idiom for jealousy, above all a lover’s or a rival’s. Sun Xiuqing calls her senior sister’s show of fairness sour with it; hence Ma Xiuzhen’s indignant ‘You mean to say I’m jealous?’

An allusion to the Short Song (短歌行) of Cao Cao (155–220): ‘Facing the wine, one should sing; for how long can a life last? It is like the morning dew, and the days already gone are all too many.’ Life as dew — bright, and burned off within the hour — is among the oldest images in Chinese poetry, and gives Dugu Yihe’s dying cry its weight.

ch10.anchor: his own swallow had flown away
ch10.note: Shangguan Feiyan’s given name, Feiyan (飞燕), means ‘flying swallow,’ and the chapter’s title, ‘The Flying Swallow Comes and Goes’ (飞燕去来), plays upon it. The swallow is the bird of the fourth month, returning each spring to the eaves it left; that Hua Manlou’s swallow should come only to fly away again, in the very season of homecoming, is the chapter’s quiet cruelty.

ch11.anchor: little Phoenix, turn back. Turn not back
ch11.note: The threat-verse is built on a pun. Each name in it holds the character 凤, ‘phoenix’: Danfeng (丹凤, ‘scarlet phoenix’) is the Princess, and ‘little Phoenix’ (小凤, Xiaofeng) is Lu Xiaofeng’s own name. The four lines run, in plain sense: the Princess you cannot win; Lu Xiaofeng, turn back — and if you will not turn back, your life will not be kept.

Daughter’s Red (女儿红) is a Shaoxing rice wine named for an old custom: a family would bury a jar of it at a daughter’s birth and dig it up, long-aged, to drink at her wedding. The name stands for the finest and most lovingly kept of wines; for Lu Xiaofeng to know it at a sip is a connoisseur’s stroke.

ch11.anchor: what he practises is the Virgin-Body discipline
ch11.note: The ‘Virgin-Body discipline’ (童子功, tongzigong, literally ‘boy’s skill’) is a strain of internal martial art that must be begun in childhood and kept only through lifelong celibacy, on the belief that an unspent vital essence can be forged into extraordinary inner power. The lore that it makes a man an eternal bachelor, and the sly banter it draws from the two friends, both turn on that price.

The ‘slow slicing’ (凌迟, lingchi), often Englished ‘death by a thousand cuts,’ was the gravest and most drawn-out of the old imperial death-penalties, reserved for treason and parricide: the condemned was put to death by many small cuts over a long while. That one of the mad ‘kings’ should threaten it lends his play-acting a genuine imperial menace.

‘The red dust’ (红尘, hongchen) is a Buddhist and Taoist figure for the mortal world — its cities, its strivings, its clamour of desire — the dust that the seeker of the Way leaves behind. To say the din of the red dust is shut off beyond the green hills is to feel, for a moment, the stillness of the renunciant.
